problem: Learned robot navigation policies may not align with human intentions and preferences (value misalignment): visual imitation fails under egocentric viewpoint mismatch, off-road navigation needs costly terrain labels or constrained demonstrations, and social navigation lacks real robot datasets and safe learned planners.
motivation: Poorly specified objectives make robots trample flowers, cut through crowds, or become overly cautious, which can be unsafe and get robots banned from public spaces. Human demonstrations and preference feedback are practical ways to convey intent, but they must be made usable with cheap data, physically different demonstrators, and novel terrains.
key_idea: Align mobile-robot navigation with human intentions and preferences via learning from demonstrations (VOILA keypoint-based reward, SCAND dataset with a classical/learned hybrid planner) and learning from preferences (STERLING/PATERN self-supervised terrain representations).
insight: Off-the-shelf viewpoint-robust keypoint matching gives a usable imitation reward across embodiments. Classical planners already match human demonstrations in up to about 80% of SCAND scenarios, so a learned planner (BC) is needed only for the hard cases. The hybrid approach avoids BC's out-of-distribution degradation while beating pure classical planning on the challenging scenarios.
method: VOILA: visual imitation from video-only demonstrations of a physically different agent; the reward is the density of SuperPoint keypoint matches between the agent's observation and the nearest demonstration image, optimized with off-policy RL, so it tolerates egocentric viewpoint mismatch.

STERLING: non-contrastive self-supervised terrain representation learning from unconstrained multimodal robot experience, followed by operator preference queries to fit a terrain preference utility used in a sampling-based planner.
PATERN: extends STERLING by extrapolating operator preferences to visually novel terrains that feel similar in proprioceptive/inertial signals to known terrains.

SCAND: dataset of 138 teleoperated socially compliant trajectories (about 40 km, 522 min) on Jackal and Spot with LiDAR/RGB-D/odometry and 12 social-interaction tags; used for BC of global and local planners.
Hybrid social planner: a learned classifier gates between move_base and a BC planner trained only on the scenarios where move_base deviates from the demonstration by more than a threshold epsilon.

setting.backbone: Task-specific networks trained from scratch: RL policy with SuperPoint reward (VOILA), self-supervised terrain encoders (STERLING/PATERN), CNN+MLP BC planners and gating classifier (SCAND)
setting.training_data: Video/LiDAR demonstrations and robot experience, SCAND (138 trajectories), and self-collected off-road robot traces; no internet-scale data
setting.observation: Egocentric RGB or LiDAR (VOILA), RGB + proprioception/inertial (STERLING/PATERN), BEV LiDAR + odometry/IMU (SCAND planners)
setting.action_space: Low-level continuous linear/angular velocity commands (or planner arcs/global paths)
setting.simulator: Simulation for VOILA plus real-world experiments

numbers_note: Dissertation on real-robot navigation (VOILA, STERLING, PATERN, SCAND); no standard embodied-navigation benchmark from the canonical list was evaluated. Much of the middle of the text (VOILA and off-road experiments) was omitted from this input. Results appear in the provided tables as Hausdorff distance, success counts, preference alignment and Likert scores, not benchmark SR/SPL.
results: VOILA-lidar achieves a Hausdorff distance of 0.487 versus 1.192 for a random policy; with viewpoint mismatch VOILA scores 0.783. STERLING succeeds 5/5 in all 7 off-road environments, matching the fully supervised baseline without terrain labels and beating RCA, GANav and SER. BC on SCAND was rated more socially compliant (4.39 vs 2.86) and safer (4.71 vs 2.89) than move_base, and the hybrid planner was generally preferred over classical or BC in the Jackal and Spot human studies.
limitations: BC assumes a unimodal behavior distribution and degrades out of distribution, and the hybrid mostly falls back on the classical planner in easy scenarios.
SCAND was collected in a single city and may carry regional norms; evaluation of social compliance is subjective and the human studies are small.
STERLING/PATERN handle only a limited set of terrains and need manually tuned balancing between geometric and preference costs.
